intro: Every day your body defends you, and every day you make choices that help it. When you scrape a knee, an army of cells rushes to clean and repair it. When a cold virus gets in, your body learns its name tag and remembers it. At the same time, you decide what to eat, when to sleep, and what to say when someone offers you something risky.

This unit has two parts. First, you will explore the immune system: the skin and mucus that block germs, the cells that eat invaders, the antibodies and memory cells that learn, and how vaccines and whole communities stay protected. Second, you will look at choices that help a growing body and brain, from food, sleep and exercise to handling peer pressure, stress and hard moments.

By the end, you will be able to explain how your body fights germs and how scientists found this out. You will be able to use facts, not fear, to think about vaping, alcohol and other drugs. You will practice refusal skills and calming skills. And you will know who to ask for help, including the 988 Lifeline.
bigQuestion: How does your body protect you, and how can your choices help it?

timeline.t: Roman writer Celsus lists four signs of inflammation: redness, heat, swelling and pain
Edward Jenner tests cowpox material to protect against smallpox
Pasteur and Koch show that specific germs cause specific diseases
Élie Metchnikoff observes cells gathering around a thorn and names phagocytes
Metchnikoff and Paul Ehrlich share the Nobel Prize for work on immunity
The World Health Assembly declares smallpox eradicated
The USDA introduces MyPlate as a guide to healthy eating
The U.S. Surgeon General reports on e-cigarettes and young people
New U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines advise 60 minutes a day for ages 6 to 17
The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline launches across the United States

words.d: a slippery, sticky fluid that lines the nose and airways and traps germs
the body's response to injury or infection, causing redness, warmth, swelling and pain
a white blood cell that swallows and destroys germs
a molecule on a germ that the immune system recognizes like a name tag
a Y-shaped protein made by B cells that locks onto one antigen
a long-lived immune cell that helps the body respond fast if a germ returns

clear, practiced ways to say no to something you do not want to do

test.q: Which is the body's first line of defense against germs?
test.why: Skin and mucus are barriers that block most germs from entering.

test.q: What causes the redness and warmth of inflammation?
choices: Widened blood vessels bringing more blood
test.why: Chemical signals widen blood vessels, so more warm blood flows to the area.
Phagocyte means eating cell; they swallow germs and debris.
B cells that meet their matching antigen become antibody factories.

test.q: Why does a second infection with the same germ often cause no illness?
choices: Memory cells respond faster and stronger
The germ gets weaker every year
test.why: Memory cells remember the antigen and launch a fast secondary response.

test.q: What was Edward Jenner's 1796 test based on?
choices: A thorn in a starfish larva
An observation that milkmaids with cowpox seemed not to catch smallpox
test.why: Jenner tested the farm observation linking cowpox to protection from smallpox.

test.q: Why does measles need about 95 percent of people immune for herd immunity?
choices: It is one of the most contagious diseases
test.why: The more contagious a germ, the higher the share of people who must be immune.

test.q: How does an allergy differ from an autoimmune condition?
choices: Only allergies involve the immune system
An allergy reacts to a harmless outside thing; autoimmunity targets the body's own cells
test.why: Allergies overreact to things like pollen; autoimmune conditions target self.

test.q: Which scientist first described phagocytes after an experiment with a thorn?
test.why: In 1882 Metchnikoff saw cells gather around a thorn in a starfish larva.

test.q: How much sleep do experts recommend for teens ages 13 to 18?
test.why: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 8 to 10 hours for teens.

test.q: How much daily physical activity do U.S. guidelines advise for ages 6 to 17?
test.why: The 2018 Physical Activity Guidelines advise 60 minutes or more daily.

test.q: Which part of the brain keeps developing into the mid-20s?
test.why: The prefrontal cortex, which helps with planning and self-control, keeps developing into the mid-20s.

choices: Saying no clearly and suggesting something else
Keeping quiet and hoping it stops
test.why: Saying no clearly, giving a short reason and suggesting another activity are refusal steps.

test.q: What can slow breathing help with?
choices: Calming a racing heart during stress
test.why: Slow breathing is a coping skill that can slow the heart and calm the body.

test.q: Who can you reach by calling or texting 988?
choices: Trained counselors at the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
test.why: 988 connects people to trained counselors, free, any time.

write.prompt: Should every middle school teach both how the immune system works and refusal skills in the same health unit? Take a position. Use at least three facts from this unit, such as how vaccines build memory, herd immunity, the developing teen brain or survey data on vaping, and explain how they support your claim.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence at the start.
Name where each fact comes from, like the CDC survey or Jenner's test.
Use unit terms such as memory cell, herd immunity and refusal skills.
Give one fair point from the other side, then explain your answer to it.
